name: Inborn errors of bile acid synthesis
aliases: congenital defects of bile acid synthesis

reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A group of autosomal recessive disorders in which enzymes converting cholesterol to the primary bile acids are deficient
The commonest defects involve 3-beta-hydroxy-delta-5-C27-steroid oxidoreductase (HSD3B7) and delta-4-3-oxosteroid 5-beta-reductase (AKR1D1)
Typically present as neonatal cholestasis with conjugated jaundice, hepatomegaly and failure to thrive, or as later progressive cholestatic liver disease of unknown cause
A distinctive feature is cholestasis with low or normal serum gamma-glutamyl transferase and characteristically low total serum bile acids, because normal bile acids are not being made
Deficient primary bile acids impair bile flow and fat and fat-soluble vitamin absorption, while accumulating atypical bile acid intermediates are hepatotoxic
The biochemical hallmark is detection of abnormal bile acid intermediates in urine by mass spectrometry, which is the key diagnostic test

Many respond dramatically to oral primary bile acid replacement (e.g. cholic acid or chenodeoxycholic acid), which restores bile flow, suppresses toxic intermediates and can avert liver transplantation
reference.pathophysiology: The synthesis of primary bile acids from cholesterol requires a sequence of enzymatic modifications to the sterol ring and side chain. In these inborn errors, deficiency of a specific enzyme in the pathway prevents formation of normal cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid and causes accumulation of upstream sterol and bile acid intermediates. The lack of normal bile acids reduces the osmotic driving force for bile flow, producing cholestasis and malabsorption of fat and fat-soluble vitamins, while the abnormal intermediates that build up are themselves hepatotoxic and drive progressive liver injury. Because the accumulating intermediates fail to suppress the pathway through feedback, provision of primary bile acids both downregulates their production and restores bile flow.
additionalDifferentials: Biliary atresia and other structural causes of neonatal cholestasis
Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (bile transporter defects)
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and other metabolic liver diseases
Neonatal infection or sepsis causing cholestasis
Peroxisomal disorders affecting bile acid synthesis
Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (a distinct bile acid synthesis defect)
additionalInvestigations: Urinary bile acid analysis by mass spectrometry to identify abnormal intermediates
Serum total bile acids (characteristically low despite cholestasis)
Serum gamma-glutamyl transferase (often normal or low)
Liver function tests and coagulation reflecting fat-soluble vitamin status
Molecular genetic testing of the relevant genes (e.g. HSD3B7, AKR1D1, CYP7B1)
Liver biopsy in selected cases to characterise the hepatopathy
redFlags: Progressive neonatal or infantile cholestasis with coagulopathy from vitamin K deficiency
Advancing liver disease or failure without an identified structural cause
Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency with bleeding, rickets or neurological signs
Delay in starting bile acid replacement in a potentially treatable liver disease
reference.prognosis: Several of these disorders are highly treatable, and timely primary bile acid replacement can normalise liver biochemistry and prevent progression to cirrhosis or transplantation; delayed diagnosis may allow irreversible liver failure to develop.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis because serum bile acids are low rather than high, which seems counterintuitive in cholestasis
Not sending specialist urinary bile acid analysis in unexplained neonatal cholestasis
Confusing a treatable synthesis defect with untreatable cholestatic disease
Missing fat-soluble vitamin deficiency and associated coagulopathy
Failing to consider these disorders in the low-GGT cholestasis group alongside transporter defects
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Oral primary bile-acid replacement with cholic acid, sometimes combined with chenodeoxycholic acid, to restore bile flow and suppress hepatotoxic intermediate production
Supplementation of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K to correct malabsorption
Nutritional support to address steatorrhoea and failure to thrive
Monitor liver biochemistry, coagulation and urinary bile-acid intermediates to confirm response and titrate replacement
Liver transplantation for those presenting late with established cirrhosis or liver failure unresponsive to replacement
Hepatology and metabolic multidisciplinary care with early treatment to prevent irreversible liver injury
Genetic counselling and family testing for autosomal recessive inheritance of genes such as HSD3B7, AKR1D1 and CYP7B1
